article.overview: An optical telescope is an instrument that collects light from astronomical sources and forms an image or spectrum of them. Placed on the Moon, a telescope avoids the blurring and absorption caused by Earth's atmosphere and can observe the sky, and the Earth's upper atmosphere, from an airless site. Only a few telescopes have operated on the lunar surface. The best-documented examples, the Apollo 16 Far Ultraviolet Camera/Spectrograph [1][2] and the Chang'e-3 Lunar-based Ultraviolet Telescope [5], both observed at ultraviolet wavelengths rather than in visible light. A lunar visible-light interferometer, MoonLITE [6], has been proposed but is not confirmed to have flown. The payload is therefore best understood as a class of lunar astronomical instruments rather than a single standard design.
article.description: An optical telescope on the Moon combines a light-collecting element (a mirror, a lens or both), a detector that records the focused light, a pointing mechanism, and thermal and power systems that keep the instrument within its operating range. The detector may be photographic film, as on Apollo 16, or an electronic CCD, as on Chang'e-3. Because the Moon has no atmosphere, the telescope observes the sky without atmospheric distortion, but it must survive the lunar day-night cycle and large temperature swings. Lunar telescopes so far have been single-purpose instruments, and each has a different wavelength band, aperture and operating method.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: Lunar telescopes are intended to observe objects that are hard to study from Earth's surface with the same stability. The Apollo 16 camera was designed to study the Earth's upper atmosphere and geocorona, the interplanetary medium and celestial objects [2], including the ultraviolet colours of stars, nebulae and diffuse gas [3]. The Chang'e-3 LUT was used to constrain the water content of the sunlit lunar exosphere, as its published title states [5]. The MoonLITE concept aims to measure the sizes of young stellar objects and probe the inner regions of active galactic nuclei by interferometry; these goals are reported in secondary coverage of the proposal and were not confirmed in the paper text read [6].
article.operating_principle: A telescope gathers light with a primary optical element and focuses it onto a detector. The Apollo 16 instrument was an F/1, 3-inch Schmidt camera whose image was amplified electronographically and recorded on nuclear emulsion film [3]. The Chang'e-3 LUT used a 150 mm F/3.75 Ritchey-Chretien telescope that fed a UV-enhanced CCD at its Nasmyth focus, with a flat mirror on a two-axis gimbal for pointing [5]. An interferometer such as MoonLITE combines light from two separated telescopes, so that its angular resolution is set mainly by the separation between them rather than by the size of either telescope [6].
article.scientific_importance: Telescopes on the Moon avoid the absorption and blurring caused by Earth's atmosphere, which is valuable for ultraviolet work in particular. The Apollo 16 camera showed that an astronaut-deployed observatory could make astronomical and Earth observations from the lunar surface [1][2]. The Chang'e-3 LUT showed that a robotic ultraviolet telescope could operate on the lunar surface for an extended period, with its team reporting highly stable photometric performance over the first six months and more than 130,000 images by the end of 2014 [5]. An interferometer would extend lunar observation to much finer angular detail than a single small telescope can provide [6]. These results support the lunar surface as an observing platform, but they do not yet establish a flown visible-light lunar telescope with a demonstrated magnitude limit.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for an optical telescope payload. The examples below are historical and proposed instruments with different wavelengths, optics and operating methods. Their values are not directly comparable and should not be read as a standard design.

examples.name: Apollo 16 Far Ultraviolet Camera/Spectrograph
examples.flight_status: Flown: set up on the Moon in April 1972 and operated 21 to 23 April 1972.
examples.optical_system: F/1, 3-inch Schmidt camera on an altitude-azimuth frame
examples.detector: Electronographic amplification recorded on nuclear emulsion film with a film transport mechanism
examples.wavelength_band: Reported as 500 to 1500 angstroms in secondary summaries; not confirmed in the primary documents read
examples.mass_note: Secondary summaries give about 50 lb (roughly 22 kg); not confirmed from a primary specification.
examples.dimensions_note: Overall dimensions of the reconstructed back-up engineering model (serial number 4) in the Smithsonian record. This is not the flown instrument.
examples.power: Not publicly specified in the sources read.

examples.name: Chang'e-3 Lunar-based Ultraviolet Telescope (LUT)
examples.flight_status: Flown: launched 2 December 2013 on a Long March-3B; first light 16 December 2013; more than 130,000 images by the end of 2014. Secondary coverage reported operation in 2017; current status not verified.
examples.optical_design: 150 mm F/3.75 Ritchey-Chretien telescope; flat mirror on a two-axis gimbal (design values)
examples.detector: UV-enhanced AIMO CCD E2V 47-20, 13 micrometre pixels, 1024 x 1024 active pixels, at the Nasmyth focus (design)
examples.throughput: Peak about 8 per cent at 2500 angstroms; effective FWHM 1080 angstroms; measured in the laboratory before launch
examples.thermal_control: Detector can be thermoelectrically cooled up to 40 C below its environment (design); images analysed were taken at a fixed CCD temperature of -40 C (operational setting)
examples.magnitude_limit: Not stated; the paper reports count-rate and column-density upper limits instead
examples.dimensions: Not stated in the paper read

examples.name: MoonLITE (Lunar InTerferometry Explorer)
examples.flight_status: Proposed; not confirmed flown. Secondary news coverage reports the 2023 proposal was not selected and a resubmission was considered; current status not verified.
examples.configuration: Two-element interferometer: a lander-mounted inboard telescope and a rover-deployed outboard telescope about 100 m away
examples.wavelength_band: Visible (the only band named in the sources read)
examples.limiting_magnitude: About 17th magnitude in the visible (stated target sensitivity)
examples.angular_resolution: Sub-milliarcsecond science claimed in the paper page read; no absolute figure given there. A limiting resolution of 110 microarcseconds reported in a secondary summary is unconfirmed.
examples.telescope_size: Not stated in the sources read
examples.power: Not stated in the sources read

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: The Apollo 16 camera's reconstructed back-up engineering model measures 49.5 x 78.7 x 53.3 cm overall, which is a Smithsonian record of a back-up model and not the flown instrument. The Chang'e-3 LUT paper does not state its dimensions, and the MoonLITE paper abstract page does not state telescope size. Dimensions for these instruments are therefore not comparable.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: The flown Apollo 16 mass is not confirmed in the primary documents read; secondary summaries give about 50 lb. Neither the Chang'e-3 LUT paper nor the MoonLITE paper abstract page gives a mass.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Not publicly specified in the sources read for the Apollo camera, the Chang'e-3 LUT or the MoonLITE concept.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A lunar optical telescope must operate without an atmosphere and through large surface temperature swings. The Apollo 16 camera was placed in the shadow of the lunar module [1], and secondary summaries say this helped limit heating and glare. The Chang'e-3 LUT detector was operated at a fixed CCD temperature of -40 degrees Celsius for the images analysed, and its design allows the detector to be cooled up to 40 degrees below its environment [5]. The sources read do not describe how these instruments handled the lunar night, dust on optics or pointing stability; these are evidence gaps for any new instrument.
article.limitations: The historical examples are not visible-light telescopes: the Apollo camera and the LUT both observed at ultraviolet wavelengths [1][5]. Both were single instruments with small apertures (a 3-inch camera and a 150 mm telescope), so their sensitivity and angular resolution are modest compared with major observatories. The Apollo camera depended on photographic film and astronaut operation, which limit scale and automation. Any lunar telescope must also survive the lunar day-night cycle, thermal extremes and dust.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: Surface telescopes can be delivered as part of a lander payload or carried by astronauts or a rover, and the three examples used different routes. Shared stages such as Earth integration, launch and lunar transfer are not described in detail in the sources read.
transportation_process: Integrate the instrument with its lander or carrier on Earth (not described in detail in the sources read).
Launch and transfer to the Moon (not described in detail in the sources read).
Deliver to the surface by a lander, or carry it on the mission; the Apollo 16 camera was carried and set up by astronauts.
Deploy and align the instrument; the Apollo 16 camera was set up on a tripod, and the MoonLITE concept uses a rover to place its outboard telescope about 100 m away.
Connect power and data, and protect the instrument thermally; details for these examples are not described in the sources read.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Apollo 16: astronaut John Young set up the camera on a tripod in the Descartes highlands, in the shadow of the lunar module [1][3]. Chang'e-3 LUT: the LUT operated from the Chang'e-3 lander, but mounting and deployment details are not stated in the paper read [5]. MoonLITE: a lander-mounted inboard telescope plus a rover-deployed outboard telescope about 100 m away [6].
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: Apollo 16 flew in April 1972 as part of the Apollo lunar surface programme [1][2]. The LUT was launched in December 2013 on a Chinese lunar mission [5]. MoonLITE is a proposed commercial-lander mission [6].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No lander, rover or spacecraft compatibility is asserted in this article. MoonLITE is designed around CLPS delivery [6], but no verified interface data for any named lander or rover was found.

article.historical_significance: NASA describes the Apollo 16 camera as the first Moon-based observatory [1]. The 1973 Applied Optics report on the instrument described the lunar surface as a potential base for astronomical observation [2]. Secondary coverage describes the Chang'e-3 LUT as the first robotic astronomical telescope working on the lunar surface; its team publications document the first-light date and long operating record [5]. Together these instruments show that the lunar surface has been used for astronomical observation, though neither was a visible-light telescope in the sense of the payload name.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: The category name 'optical telescope' describes a broad class, and the examples here cover ultraviolet instruments and one proposed visible-light interferometer. Values such as mass, power, magnitude limit and wavelength band must always be tied to a named instrument and source. Several values for the Apollo camera and the LUT are not stated in the sources read, and the Apollo mass and wavelength figures from secondary summaries are unconfirmed. The MoonLITE status and resolution figures come from a proposal and secondary coverage. This article is not a certified design specification for a new payload.

data_quality_notes: Optical telescope class: the lunar examples verified in this run are ultraviolet instruments (Apollo 16 FUV camera, Chang'e-3 LUT). No flown visible-band lunar telescope was confirmed in the sources reviewed.

Apollo 16 mass (about 50 lb / roughly 22 kg) and wavelength band (500 to 1500 angstroms) come from secondary summaries and were not confirmed in primary documents. They are recorded as unverified; mass_kg is null.
The Apollo 16 dimensions are those of a reconstructed back-up engineering model (serial number 4), not the flown unit.
The Chang'e-3 LUT paper (ar5iv rendering of arXiv:1502.04287) does not state mass, size, power or magnitude limit. The arXiv PDF could not be read as text, so the ar5iv HTML rendering was used.

MoonLITE: the 2023 non-selection and possible resubmission come from secondary news coverage. The 110 microarcsecond resolution figure is from a secondary summary; the paper page read gave no absolute resolution value.

Image verification is incomplete: the NASA image URL was taken from the NASA source page during research and was not visually inspected or checked for resolution. Smithsonian image asset URLs were not verified, so image_url is null for that item.
Other lunar optical concepts seen in search results (for example AeSI and a Schneider and Labeyrie optical telescope proposal) were not researched in depth and are not covered by this article.
Web search and fetch were used under the frugal research budget; the Apollo 16 Applied Optics full reprint was not read, so hardware specifications remain partly unverified.
